verses.note: The verse promises an inward change done by God, not a new rule set before the old heart. Augustine built his argument in On the Spirit and the Letter (about 412) on this passage: the law written on stone commands, while the law written on the heart by God's Spirit gives the love that fulfills it.

Cleansing comes first, and it is God's act: I will sprinkle, I will cleanse. Psalm 51:7 had prayed for exactly this. The verse joins forgiveness (removal of defilement) and renewal (the heart and spirit that follow) as two sides of one work.

This verse is one of the main Old Testament foundations of the doctrine of regeneration, God's giving new life to the inner person. The command of 18:31 (‘make yourselves a new heart’) and the promise here are both Scripture: the obligation is real, and God himself supplies what he commands. Augustine's prayer in the Confessions (10.29), asking God to give what he commands, states the same logic.
Good fruit comes from a good tree. The image teaches that conduct flows from what a person is, which is why Jesus elsewhere says the tree itself must be made good (12:33).
Behavior flows from what a person is. The verse implies that changing fruit requires changing the tree, the renewal of the heart that the prophets promised (Ezekiel 36:26).

‘Dead’ and ‘alive again’ are the father's words for estrangement and return, not literal death. The New Testament letters take up the same language for new birth: God made us alive together with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses (Ephesians 2:4-5).

Verse 13 is the Bible's clearest statement that new birth is God's work. It rules out three routes a first-century reader might trust: ancestry, natural desire, and human decision. Faith receives the gift (verse 12); God is the one who begets (verse 13).

Jesus makes new birth the condition of seeing God's kingdom, and the passive verb makes it God's work. The kingdom is not reached by improving the old life but by receiving a new one from above, as 1:13 had already said.
Only the Spirit gives birth to spirit. The new life is not natural life improved but a life with a new source, which is why John can call believers born of God (1:13, 1 John 5:1).
The word must places new birth among the things God has ordained, alongside the cross (verse 14). It is not an option for the especially spiritual but the condition of life for everyone.
Eternal life is not only a future reward but a present possession, received through hearing and believing. The new birth of chapter 3 is described here as a passage from death to life.
People are called ‘the dead’ before they hear the Son's voice. Life comes by his word, as it came to the dead man at Bethany. The verse makes spiritual life the Son's gift, not a human achievement.

The disciples' cleanness is the gift of Jesus' word, received in faith, not the result of their own effort. The New Testament elsewhere joins the word and cleansing in the same way: Christ cleanses the church by the washing of water with the word (Ephesians 5:26), and believers are born again through the living word of God (1 Peter 1:23).

True circumcision is an inward work of the Spirit on the heart. Paul points to what later theology calls regeneration, the renewal God promised in Deuteronomy 30:6 and Ezekiel 36:26-27, which no ritual can produce.

‘From the heart’ and ‘thanks be to God’ together say that genuine obedience was God's work in them, the new heart promised in Ezekiel 36:26-27. Paul does not thank the Romans for obeying; he thanks God.
New life is God's act on the dead, not their response to an offer. The verse joins the believer's rebirth to Christ's resurrection: the life given is his risen life shared.
Writing the law on the heart is an inward renewal of desire and understanding. The promise describes what the New Testament calls new birth: God himself changes the heart from within.
